decision: PARTIAL -> W1 + W6: today's [2,4] is a Clemson lo + USU hi blend across two pages. clemson_hgic turnips-rutabagas (covers turnip and rutabaga jointly) states "Space plants 2 to 3 inches apart in the row." -> in_row [2,3]; "Plant in rows that are 14 to 18 inches apart." -> row [14,18]. USU's 'thin turnips 3-4 inches between plants in rows 12-18 inches apart' is the alternative. Eleven prose strings restating 2-4 are re-authored to 2-3; container notes keep their pot guidance.

edits.new: Loosen the bed and pull out rocks before planting, thin the turnips to 2 to 3 inches so they are not crowded, and skip fresh manure and heavy nitrogen feeding. On rocky or heavy soil, use a raised bed or a deep, loose container.
edits.reason: restates the moved in-row figure (Clemson: 2-3 in)

edits.new: Work the bed loose and remove stones before sowing, thin to 2 to 3 inches so roots are not crowded, and avoid fresh manure and heavy nitrogen. On heavy or rocky ground, use a raised bed or a deep, loose container.
edits.reason: restates the moved in-row figure (Clemson: 2-3 in)

edits.new: Thin the seedlings to about 2 to 3 inches apart once they are 2 to 4 inches tall, snipping the extras at the soil line. Eat the thinnings as baby greens. Keep weeds out and the soil evenly damp, and use a row cover if flea beetles are bad.
edits.reason: restates the moved in-row figure (Clemson: 2-3 in)

edits.new: Thin to a final 2 to 3 inches apart once seedlings reach 2 to 4 inches, snipping the extras at the soil line; the thinnings are edible baby greens. Keep the bed weed-free and evenly moist, and cover with row fabric if flea beetles are heavy.
edits.reason: restates the moved in-row figure (Clemson: 2-3 in)

edits.new: Once the seedlings are 2 to 4 inches tall, thin them to 2 to 3 inches apart, snipping the extras at the soil line. Eat the thinnings as baby greens. Crowded turnips stay small.
edits.reason: restates the moved in-row figure (Clemson: 2-3 in)

edits.new: Once seedlings stand 2 to 4 inches, thin to a final 2 to 3 inches apart, snipping at the soil line. The thinnings are edible baby greens. Crowded turnips stay small and misshapen.
edits.reason: restates the moved in-row figure (Clemson: 2-3 in)

edits.new: Turnips are planted a bit thick, so you need to thin them, or the crowded roots stay small and lumpy. Thin them to about 2 to 3 inches apart once they are 2 to 4 inches tall, closer together if you just want greens or small salad turnips, snipping the extra ones off at the soil line with scissors instead of pulling. Do not toss the thinnings, the little leaves are tasty baby turnip greens, so thinning is really your first harvest.
edits.reason: restates the moved in-row figure (Clemson: 2-3 in)

edits.new: Turnips are sown a little thick and must be thinned, or the crowded roots stay small and misshapen. Thin to a final 2 to 3 inches apart once seedlings reach 2 to 4 inches tall, closer for salad turnips and greens and toward 3 inches for full-size roots, snipping the extras at the soil line rather than pulling so you do not disturb the ones you keep. Do not waste the thinnings: the young leaves are tender baby turnip greens, so thinning is also a first small harvest.
edits.reason: restates the moved in-row figure (Clemson: 2-3 in); the 'wider (3 to 4 inches)' clause (USU) is re-authored to 'toward 3 inches'

edits.new: Thin the turnips to about 2 to 3 inches apart once they are 2 to 4 inches tall, snipping the extras at the soil line instead of pulling, so you do not disturb the ones you keep. Crowded turnips stay small. Plant closer if you just want greens.
edits.reason: restates the moved in-row figure (Clemson: 2-3 in)

edits.new: Thin to a final 2 to 3 inches once seedlings reach 2 to 4 inches, snipping at the soil line rather than pulling to spare the keepers' roots. Crowded turnips stay small and misshapen; closer spacing suits salad and greens types.
edits.reason: restates the moved in-row figure (Clemson: 2-3 in)

edits.new: One root per plant, plus a flush of edible leaves along the way. Yield is best thought of by row length: at a 2 to 3 inch final spacing, a 10-foot row yields roughly 5 to 10 pounds of roots depending on size at harvest, alongside greens taken as outer leaves and thinnings. A greens-only crop yields more leaf per foot of row.
edits.reason: restates the moved in-row figure (Clemson: 2-3 in)
